newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australia retail, building data.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australia retail, building data.

text.p: Australian retail trade rose 2.7 percent in January, while building approvals for the same month jumped 10.4 percent, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reported on Tuesday.
Median forecasts had centred on respective rises of 1.5 and 2.0 percent, having both fallen 1.0 percent in December.
A selection of economists' immediate reactions to the data follows.
NIGEL STAPLEDON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, WESTPAC BANKING CORP:

"Net exports is quite a bit higher than we expected. It confirms our view that there will only be a small rise in GDP and must raise the prosepct of a slight negative in GDP for the December quarter. The rebound in retail sales is only marginally above what we were expecting. We have had some very weak numbers which probably overstated the weakness in the December quarter, so we have a strong rebound which is line with most of the anecdotal evidence, but off a very low base. There will be some aberration in the building approvals number, but at the very least it confirms the upward trend which started emerging late last year."
MICHAEL BLYTHE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, COMMONWEALTH BANK:

"It's just continuing the run of data which has come in at the stronger end of expectations over the last month or so. In some ways it doesn't cause anything new in the sense that the housing recovery is on track, but it may perhaps be picking up a little bit more strongly than we were generally thinking. I suppose the good news is...that after a period of weakness, it looks like the consumer has come back. It reinforces the message that the RBA has been pushing for a few weeks now that don't look for any more rate cuts for the time being."
CHRIS CATON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST:

"It does appear that we've turned a corner. That growth which spent most of the last 12 months slowing down is now about to go the other way. Over the past year, we've probably grown by little more than two percent. And over the next year, pushed along by the housing sector and by retail trade, we could manage four percent growth. The net export contribution detraction in the December quarter was a lot bigger than we thought it was going to be. So that pulls down our December quarter growth forecast from 0.7 percent to 0.5 percent."
ANNETTE BEACHER, SENIOR ECONOMIST, CITIBANK AUSTRALIA:

"On first view, the fact that both of them are up is great news for strengthening the economy in 1997, we have definitely seen the worst. It shows that the anecdotes from the retailers that they had had good sales in January have obviously filtered through to real data, and it also bodes well for February. These same people also said that February sales were up as well. Today's data confirms that we have seen the worst of it in the December quarter and away we go for Q1."
JOHN EDWARDS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, HSBC MARKETS:

"The retail sales is stronger than we expected. There's no doubt some errors in seasonality have influenced it, but it's nevertheless a very strong number. The markets have reacted accordingly and similarly with building approvals. Our view is that the chances of an interest rate cut were anyway minimal, but equally the chances of near-term interest rate increases are also minimal, so we don't expect it to have any impact on monetary policy."
DAVID DE GARIS: SENIOR TREASURY ECONOMIST, ANZ BANK:

"It (the retail trade outcome) gives a little bit more substance to the employment numbers that we saw in the December quarter because there was quite a wedge between what the employment numbers were telling us and what the retail trade numbers were telling us. So it sets consumer spending off to a pretty good start to the end of the March quarter. Clearly the monthly numbers are volatile but consumer spending is off to a good start and that should give us a bit of confidence that the economy is close to its turning point, if not past it. I think (the Reserve Bank) would be looking to see whether the economy is passing its low point and that certainly appears to be the case. So there is
HANS KUNNEN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, COLONIAL STATE BANK:

"Single houses actually fell, all the growth is in units and town house type developments. So it's not pointing to a rise in individual consumer optimism, rather it is the developers, the professionals of the housing market, that are seeing this as a good time to develop. Retail sales could be anything. It could have been waiting for January sales, it could be seasonal adjustment problems. All it does say to us is that the March quarter GDP figures are on a very sound footing."
